blocks.x: Learners at different levels need different teaching. This article uses three simple labels: beginner, intermediate and advanced. The Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR) describes levels from A1 to C2. Beginner is about A1 to A2, intermediate about B1 to B2, and advanced about C1 to C2.

blocks.x: In behaviour psychology, positive punishment has a technical meaning. It does not mean a nice or kind punishment.

The terms come from operant conditioning, associated with the psychologist B. F. Skinner. Positive means something is added. Negative means something is removed. Reinforcement increases a behaviour. Punishment decreases a behaviour.

head: Term
What happens
Effect on behaviour
Classroom example
rows: Praise or a point for finishing homework
The teacher stops repeating reminders once learners start working quietly
Losing a few minutes of free time

items: Punishment may stop a behaviour for a short time, but it does not teach learners what to do instead.
It can cause fear, anger, or avoidance of the teacher or the subject.
How well it works depends on timing, consistency and the relationship between teacher and learner.
Harsh punishment, public humiliation and physical punishment can harm learners. They are not recommended.
Reinforcing the behaviour you want usually leads to longer-lasting change.
Stay calm. Speak privately when you can.
Keep the consequence proportionate and related to the behaviour.
Explain it in advance so it is not a surprise.
Be consistent.
Focus on the behaviour, not the learner's character.
Give the learner a chance to put things right.
Never use physical or humiliating punishments.
Avoid using schoolwork, such as extra homework, as punishment, because it teaches learners to dislike the work.

head: Instead of
Try
rows: A clear signal, then wait for quiet
A short talk, or a catch-up task related to the missed work
Embarrassing a learner in front of others
A private word, or moving a seat

Give praise or rewards soon after the behaviour.
